x=2cos⁡θ+4,y=2sin⁡θ−3
c
x=4cos⁡θ+2,y=4sin⁡θ−3

e
x=4cos⁡θ−3,y=4sin⁡θ+2

decision.explanation: The standard parametrization is x=4+2cos(θ), y=-3+2sin(θ). At θ=0 it starts at (6,-3), and as θ increases it moves upward, counterclockwise, completing one circle over [0,2π).

after.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r+a,b).$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(4,-3).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -3,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Consider the circle of radius 2 centered at (4,−3), as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point A(6,−3)?

a
x=2sin⁡θ+3,y=2cos⁡θ−4

x=2cos⁡θ+4,y=2sin⁡θ−3

Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from (r+a,b).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 2 centered at the point (4,−3). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=2cos⁡θ+4,y=2sin⁡θ−3,θ∈[0,2π).

$$

$$

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -3,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

after.problem:

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
after.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =49({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =49(1) \\  & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
content.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =49({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =49(1) \\  & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=49.$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Determine the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
after.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+1}{2} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-4}{2} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y-4)^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ (x+1)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $(x+1)^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=4.$

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r+a,b).$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(2,1).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Consider the circle of radius $2$ centered at $(2,1)$, as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$  traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(4,1)?$
content.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r+a,b).$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(2,1).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

after.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in (0,2\pi ].
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $1$ centered at the point $(-1,1).$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1,\,\theta \in (0,2\pi ].
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a three-quarter-circle, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the line parallel to the $x$-axis and crossing the center of the circle. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14011969/assets/28d5eaee4de3a6100a92fa017b71d9860ea19cd7073284b41511dda4155ecb6d.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[\frac{\pi }{2},2\pi ]$, we get the required three-quarter-circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the three-quarter circle are 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1,\,\theta \in [\frac{\pi }{2},2\pi ].
$$
